newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Platinum price gives Northam some respite.
newsitem.headline: Platinum price gives Northam some respite.

text.p: Current high platinum prices were making beleaguered Northam Platinum Ltd profitable but the sustainability of the recent price surge must be questioned, Northam chairman Peter Janisch said on Tuesday.

Local news reports said earlier that loss-making Northam could make a profit in the current quarter, fuelled by the platinum price's rush from a close of $399.50 an ounce on June 2 to Monday's close of $450 an ounce.
But Janish told Reuters that Northam had suffered losses in April and May and these rich platinum prices had only been enjoyed for a short while.
"It's difficult to call. We made losses in the first two months (of this quarter). If we were to go on getting this kind of price it would help us into profitability," he said.
"But how long will it (platinum price rise) last. It looks like it's falling at the moment, but it's still good for Northam," he said.
Northam deepened its pre-capex net loss in the three months to end-March, falling to a loss of 18.44 million rand from a 1.78 million rand loss in the December quarter.

World market worries about delayed Russian platinum deliveries triggered the metal price's rush higher last week. Russian platinum stockpiles hold the key to the platinum price and have held it in a tight range for years.
Escaping its territory, usually a few dollars above or below $400 an ounce, the platinum price touched a high of $500 last Friday, taking Northam up with it.
Shares rose as high as 250 cents on Friday, having started their climb with the metal from 218 cents on June 2.
Thinly traded Northam options hit 23 rand on Monday -- their closing year high -- from opening the day at 12 rand.

But on Tuesday, as platinum lost ground to below $450 an ounce, Northam shares fell eight cents to 236 cents and options were the leading losers by percentage on the JSE, dropping more than 40 percent to 10 rand.
This, analysts said, showed the market's lack of trust in the platinum price rise.

"People don't think that the price is sustainable that's why it's (Northam) softer today. People don't believe the price will hold these levels. You'll see a pullback when the Russians deliver," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
He said the price would likely stabilise around $400 and in the meantime Northam would reap all the benefits it could from higher prices.
Reporting March quarter results in April, Janisch said a platinum price above 58,000 rand per kg would help Northam realise a profit.
When platinum touched $500 its rand/kg price was around 79,400 rand/kg. Last bid at $448.50 an ounce, Northam is still winning about 71,000 rand/kg.
